IOANNIS TRITE- MII ABBATIS PEAPOLITANI ORDINIS SAN CTI BENE DICTI, POLYGRAPHIAE LIBER SECVNDVS CAPIT INITIVM. <Initial type="decorated-drop">R</Initial>ATIO numerandi mortalium, artena turam conatur imitari monadis nullũ calculũ admittentis. Vnde q̃uis insti¬ tutio libri polygraphiae pręcedẽtis ꝑ extensionem metathesinꝙ particula¬ rium, quasi ad uniuerfalia huius artis sufficiat in infinitas numeri progressiones, certa nos tamẽ consyderatio permouit, ut alterum alteri copulemus. Lu¬ cis est in utroqꝫ dispar conditio, nox uero cursus sui ordi¬ nem utrobiqꝙ iniuolatum custodit. Qui prudẽs est lector ex paruis non satis ad amussim politis adiuentionib⁹ nostris, facile maiora politioraqꝙ ingenio pręstanti si ui¬ geat poterit inuenire. Quicquid est uisibile in universo mundi circulo positum, adhuc nouae artis nostrae mini¬ sterium promtpum tribuit fulcimentum. Aer ignis, aq̃ terra, fontes flumĩa, arbores fructecta, flores gra¬ mina, uerba nomina, accidens substantia, lapides arena, fimus stercora, res uocabula, honesta uere¬ cunda, ligna metalla, dura liquida, existentia non existentia, historia fabula, bestiae bruta, homines iumenta, singula uniuerfa, quaeuelsermo potest ex¬ primere, uel anima cogitare, campum polygraphiae no¬ strae pręstant latiffimum, Artem quantum mortalibus potest constare promittunt ampliandam fore in infinitũ. Nam sicuti ex unitate per binarium ternarius perfectum numerum in quaternario generat, sic huius adiuuentio¬ nis consumatio per quaternarium in binario bis perfecto constituens radicem infinitum nobis numerum sub mi- nucijs rerum et paraphrasmatũ polygraphiae donat. Nã et amp;si apud nos omnia nostra sint terminabilia, plura tamen saepius occurrũt quae nobis propter intellectus nostri tar- ditatem uidentur infinita. Guttas maris dinumerare quis poterit: Et cor homĩs inscrutabile quis penetrabit? Quẽ- admodum finitus et amp; circumscriptibilis numerus, ꝓgressi one ducibilis est in infinitum, sic huius artis institutio ua- ria metathesi ampliatur in immensum. Quicquid uspiam in toto mundo cernitur, nostrae institutioni per omnia cõ- formatur, nec est aliq́uid nobis cognitũ quod uacet a my- sterio, si modus intelligitur a magistro. Nos autem ratio- ne persuasi sub ministerio binarij consistimus, &amp; partẽ to- tius minimam breuiter explicamus. Neqꝫ ut conatũ erige remus ad grauiora nobis datur occasio, quae si nobis offe- ratur acceptabilis, non aspernabimur potiora cupiẽtibus facere manifesta. Scriptum est enim: Vbi non est auditus ne sermonem effuderis un. Secundum igitur polygra- phiae librum adj̃cientes primo, formam ciusdem tenemꝰ et amp;modum.paraphrasmata in lumine diei octo et amp; trecẽta simplici progressione locantes pro memoria honorabili, castissimae dei genitricis, quae si tempus affuisset oportu- num et amp; uenustiora dare poteramus, &amp; sufficiente diffusio ne campestri latiora. Sed utrũqꝫ facile dabit studiosa po- steritas, ut et amp; nitorem apponat materiae, &amp; sufficientẽ pro gressum formae. Primus cuiuslibet artis inuentor maiora transmittit ad posteros, quia cum sint artis dura et amp; incon- sucta principia, nulla reperitur subtilis adinuentio ab ori- gine consummata. Ex Peapoli quae et amp; Herbipolis urbe Francorum orientalium, duodecima die mẽsis Februarij. The second book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Peapolis, of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

The human method of numbering attempts by art to imitate nature, which admits no reckoning of the monad. Therefore, although the instruction of the preceding book of Polygraphy, through extension and the metathesis of particulars, suffices, as it were, for the universals of this art in infinite progressions of number, nevertheless a definite consideration has moved us to join a second to the first.

There is in each a different condition of light, but night in both preserves inviolate the order of its course. The reader who is prudent, from our small discoveries, not polished quite to the rule, will easily be able, if he is strong in excellent talent, to discover greater and more polished things. Whatever visible thing is placed in the whole circle of the world still offers ready support to the ministry of our new art. Air, fire, water, earth, springs, rivers, trees, thickets, flowers, grasses, words, names, accident, substance, stones, sand, dung, filth, things, terms, honorable things, modest things, woods, metals, hard things, liquid things, existing things, non-existing things, history, fable, beasts, brute animals, human beings, draught-animals, each and all things that speech can express or the mind can think, provide the very broad field of our Polygraphy; they promise that the art, insofar as it can stand among mortals, is to be enlarged to infinity.

For just as unity, through the binary, generates the ternary as a perfect number in the quaternary, so the completion of this discovery, establishing its root through the quaternary in the twice-perfect binary, gives us an infinite number under the minute particulars of things and of the paraphrases of Polygraphy. For although among us all our things are terminable, yet very many things often occur which, because of the slowness of our understanding, seem infinite to us. Who will be able to count the drops of the sea? And who will penetrate the inscrutable heart of man? Just as a finite and circumscribable number can, by progression, be led into infinity, so the instruction of this art is enlarged into immensity by varied metathesis. Whatever is seen anywhere in the whole world is in all respects conformed to our instruction, nor is there anything known to us that is without mystery, if the method is understood by a master.

We, however, persuaded by reason, remain under the ministry of the binary, and briefly explain the smallest part of the whole. Nor is an occasion given us to raise our undertaking to weightier matters; if such an acceptable occasion is offered to us, we shall not refuse to make more excellent things manifest to those who desire them. For it is written: Where there is no hearing, do not ever pour out speech. Therefore, adding the second book of Polygraphy to the first, we keep the same form and method, placing three hundred and eight paraphrases in the light of day by simple progression, in honorable memory of the most chaste mother of God; if the time had been suitable, we could have given both more graceful things and, with sufficient expansive diffusion, broader things. But studious posterity will easily provide both: it will add brilliance to the matter and sufficient progress to the form. The first inventor of any art transmits greater things to posterity, because, since the beginnings of an art are hard and unfamiliar, no subtle discovery is found consummate from its origin.

From Peapolis, which is also Herbipolis, a city of the Eastern Franks, on the twelfth day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord 1508.

Of eternity. Let it be. Of felicity; of deity; of piety; of quiet; of peace; of light; of the heavenly [realm]; of the pious; of the good; of fruition; and of tranquility.

<Initial type="decorated-drop">A</Initial>VXILIANTE domino nostro Iesu Chri¬ sto, saluatore fidelium animarum, qui sacro uiuit: in unitate ternario cum patre et amp; spiri¬ tu sancto, trinus in personis, &amp; unus in sub¬ stantia deus, incomprehensibilis, omni¬po¬ tens et amp; sempiternus: a quo, in quo, &amp; per quem omne bonū pulchrum procedit et amp; uerum, secundū hunc polygraphiae librum perduximꝰ ad finem. De quo ipsi laus, honor, uir¬ tus et amp; gloria: qui per mortis suae innocētiā genus nostrū de interitu perditionis aeternae liberauit, &amp; omnibus in eū conscientia pura creditibus, aeternae uitae aditum misera¬ tione ꝑpetua rescravit. Lineatim octo et amp; trecenta parapbra smata cōsignauimus, prolixiorem euagationem picariam confilio deuitātes. Satis etenim nobis in huius lucu brationis exordio uisum est, si causam uolenti¬ bus ampliora dederimus perquirēdi, cum nobis ad ea defuerit et amp; tempus et amp; ratio. Lector amice vale. Ex Peapoli, penultima die mensis Febru arij. Anno domini Mil lesimo quingente simo octauo.</Line> <Paragraph> <Emphasis type="other">IOANNIS TRI</Emphasis> </Line>TEMII ABBATIS POLYGRAPHIAE LIBER SECVNDVS FINE CONCLVDITVR.</Line> 602</Paragraph> Kodak Gray Scale 1/32 <Initial type="decorated-drop">C</Initial>IOANNIS TRITE MII ABBATIS PEAPOLITANI ORDINIS SAN- CTI BENEDEICTI, LIBER POLYGRAPHIAE TERTIVS INITIVM SVMIT. VID aprimordio creationis humanae unitatē linguae confudit: Nonne diui- sio corporum, & uarietas animorum? Nam utueritas in euangelio protesta- tur: Exabundantia cordis os loquit̉. Lingua em̄instrumentū est eaꝝ cōce- ptionū foras proferendi, quas apud semetipsum animus in interioribus cogitauit. Huius tamen ministerij secretorū animi ad sensum plures sunt modi, quoꝝ ꝓprietates &; usu uariant̉ &; arte. Vsus ad placitū introductus, cōmunis est multis: ars uero paucis. Deniqꝫ &; usus ipse loquendi nō re- gulatus, quantum apud folos theutonicos in sexcentis an- nis fit uarius, nemo cito aestimabit, qui Otfridum Vuis- senburgensem monachū in carminibus linguae Germani- cae saepius non relegit. Mare fluit &; refluit, homines semel morientes nō amplius praesentē reuertuntur ad uitā. Succe dunt moribus mores, &; semp ad molliora uigor animorū mortaliū decidit. Quis hodie apud Graecoꝝ priscos aemu- latores germanos, antiqua idiomatū tenet noticiā? Chro- nicis &; ueterū historijs Francoꝝ Hunibaldus, Doracꝰ et reliqui scriptores, ꝗ annis nos mille praecesserunt, multa et carmine prisco &; prosa sermonis theutonici suis synthema tibus dicta miscuerunt, quaehodie intelliguntur a paucis. Quid loquor de tēporibus antiquis, cū propriū idioma no- strum apud Francos orientales, Sueuos, Bauaros, Rhenen- ses, Mosellanos, Colonienfes, Saxones &; Doringos, nota bilem quotidie uariationem suscipiat. Mutantur in tēpo-

With the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, the savior of faithful souls, who lives in the sacred triune unity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, three in persons and one God in substance, incomprehensible, almighty, and everlasting, from whom, in whom, and through whom proceeds every good, beautiful, and true thing, we have brought this second book of the Polygraphia to an end. To him be praise, honor, power, and glory: he who, through the innocence of his death, freed our race from the destruction of eternal perdition, and in perpetual mercy reopened the entrance to eternal life to all who believe in him with a pure conscience. Line by line we have set down three hundred and eight paraphrases, avoiding a more lengthy wandering [unclear]. For it seemed enough to us at the beginning of this lucubration if we had given those who wished it a reason to inquire further, since both time and method failed us for those matters. Farewell, friendly reader. From Peapolis, on the penultimate day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord one thousand five hundred and eight.

The Second Book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot, Ends with its Conclusion.

The Third Book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Peapolis, of the Order of Saint Benedict, Begins.

Why did [unclear] from the beginning of human creation confuse the unity of language? Was it not the division of bodies and the variety of minds? For as Truth testifies in the Gospel: from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. For the tongue is the instrument for bringing forth outwardly those conceptions which the mind has thought within itself in its inner parts. Yet there are several modes of this ministry of the mind’s secrets to sense, whose properties and use are varied by practice and by art. Practice, introduced at will, is common to many; but art to few. Finally, no one will readily estimate how varied even the very practice of speaking, unregulated, has become among the Germans alone in six hundred years, unless he has more than once reread Otfrid, the monk of Weissenburg, in the poems of the German language. The sea flows and ebbs; men, once dying, do not return again to present life. Customs succeed customs, and the vigor of mortal minds always falls away toward softer things. Who today, among the Germans, the ancient emulators of the Greeks, retains knowledge of the old idioms? In the chronicles and old histories of the Franks, Hunibald, Doracus, and the other writers who preceded us by a thousand years mixed into their compositions many things said both in old verse and in prose of the German language, which today are understood by few. Why do I speak of ancient times, when our own idiom among the East Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, Rhenish people, Mosellans, people of Cologne, Saxons, and Thuringians undergoes notable variation every day? They are changed in time-

71
re homines, uariantur et mores, mutantur animi, uariātur et amp; uestes: linguarū alteratur simplicitas, prisca uariatur idiomatũ proprietas, nihil stabile reperitur in humanis. Omniū em̄ uicissitudo est rerũ, succedit uarietas simpli- citati animorũ. Quis defluētiã hac, ut ita loquar, perpetuã ad cõcordiã poterit reducere unitatis? Transeunt em̄ tẽpo- ra plura ut scriptura dicit, multiplex erit scientia. Quod aūt duobus Polygraphiae libris praecedentibus tertiũ adij cimus, ratione nō caruit speciali. Nā ut cũ uarieae sint homi- nũ uoluntas, recte multiplices dantur modi ad honestas oꝑationes. In illis noctẽ dies illuminat, in istis uero dies a lumine uacat. Illic umbram lux circũducit in lumine, isthic aūt caecus caecũ illuminat, uisum sine oculis existẽs p- manens quẽ nō habet tenebris ministrat. Hic nox diẽ cali- gine perpetua obnubilat, ambulãs in tenebris sine lumi, ne caeco ducatũ praestat. Haec paraphrasmata cunctis ꝑ mū dum hominibus deseruiũt, in omni lingua quodlibet ar chanũ, tuto, secure, ac sine periculo ad cabalisticũ binariũ transmittunt. Barbaris risum mouet latinitas, suspicio, nē latinis ipsa barbaries generat. Refert tamē nihil aut parũ quoniā suspicio quaniũlibet fuerit, mysteriũ nibilominus omne secretissimum cõtinebit. Ad mentẽ regulas pręce pta quae tradidimus operator studiosus reuocet, ne inutili- ter inuanum sibi alijs laboret. Intelligentia enim opus est, sine qua nullius artis cōstabit utilitas. Iter paucis oste̓ dimus ad maxima, finitis modum dedimus ad infinita. Ex datis acceptis, facile maiora parantur amicis. Lector memento notam retrogradam in omni loco posse configi. quousque uotam apprehendas quietis. Vale, Ex Peapoli, prima die Martij. Anno domini. M. D. [People?] change, customs also vary, minds change, and garments vary; the simplicity of languages is altered, the ancient proper character of idioms is varied; nothing stable is found in human affairs. For there is change in all things; variety succeeds to simplicity of minds. Who will be able to bring this perpetual flux, so to speak, back to the concord of unity? For many times pass away, as Scripture says, and knowledge will be manifold. But the fact that we add a third book to the two preceding books of the Polygraphy has not lacked a special reason. For, since human wills are various, many methods are rightly given for honorable operations. In the former, night illuminates day; in the latter, however, day lacks light. There light leads shadow around in light; here, however, the blind man illuminates the blind, being and remaining sight without eyes, and serves to darkness what he does not possess. Here night clouds day with perpetual darkness, and, walking in darkness without light, furnishes guidance to the blind. These paraphrasmata serve all men throughout the world; in every language they transmit any secret safely, securely, and without danger to the cabalistic binary. Latin makes barbarians laugh; barbarism itself generates suspicion among Latins. Yet it matters nothing, or little, since however great the suspicion may have been, it will nonetheless contain every mystery in the utmost secrecy. Let the diligent operator recall to mind the rules and precepts that we have handed down, lest he labor uselessly and in vain for himself and for others. For understanding is needed; without it the usefulness of no art will stand. In a few words we have shown the path to the greatest things; with finite things we have given a method for infinite things. From what is given and received, greater things are easily prepared for friends. Reader, remember that the retrograde mark can be fastened in every place, until you attain the desired rest. Farewell. From Peapol, on the first day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

Noctẽ arcanis tuto seruientem, umbris periphrasma tum ducẽdam cõmisimos, numeros ordine quatuor linearum telotenus interposuimus pro usu uolentiũ adaptatos Loca sunt minutiarum gradus habentia fixos triamilia cẽtum quinquaginta, quamque horarum restent momenta si uolueris infinita, pro secretandis in omni natione lingua orbis qui cquid arcani occurrerit. Orbem linealiter nalcen tem ex puncto, quotiens nox imaginem lucis excedit, qua tũ uolueris: opus fuerit reducere poteris ad semitã qua uenisti. Si noctis super est multum, reducito caudã draconis ad caudalicium originale in caput. Verũ binarius omni nos sit certificatus de notis signaculis unitatis. Qui multũ esurit, multum laboret ut habeat quod manducet. Nec est est opus magni laboris id quo<Emphasis type="underline">r</Emphasis>sum uolueris ducere, quod sua sponte progreditur. Hic ergo finem tertio poligraphiae nostrae libro constituimus, in nomine patris filij spiritusancti. Lector mitis uale. Ex Peapolii, septima die mensis Martij. Anno domini Iesu Christi saluatoris nostri millesimo quingentesimo octauo, Inditione undecima.</Line> Adest finis tertij libri Polygraphiae Ioannis Trite mij abbatis Peapolitanj ordinis sancti Benedicti. Kodak Gray Scale IOAN·TRITEMII ABBATIS MONASTERII SANCTI IACOBI MA- ioris apostoli Vuirciburgensis, quondam Spanhei, mēsis, ordini diuis Benedicti, quartus Polygra phiae liber incipit. <Gap reason="damaged" extent="ca. 1-2 words"/> ORDO EXPOSTVLABAT rationis quartum Polygragiae nostrae librum qualitate, inuentione &; facilitate diffi- milē fieri praecedentibus: quatenus uo- lentes rerū nostra participari arcanis nō uno sed uarijs id modis asequātur atqꝫ diuersis. Extendimus picam facilima inuentione com prebensibilem, ut nox per minutiam semper coniuncta monadi quolibet ordine in lumíne cognoscatur diei. Nul- la isthic inter unitatem &; binariū reperitur differsio: neqꝫ oportebit artis instrumētum operari uolentem habere ad manum, quando primae succede is fine medio, latens osten dit mysteriū. Vnde prudens, intelligens &; expertus scien- tiam, omni tēpore &; loco, satis faciet operationi. Binarius ab unitate recipit, unde ternariū producit. Facilis ē huiꝰ cry ptologię facie prima cognitio: postea q̃ luna uel puncto u- rico fuerit a sole illustrata. Qͣuis &; fieri possit ꝙ gnosticꝰ euadat industrius sine manuductione magistri. Quod in isto tamen libro tantū reor intelligendū, in praecedentiū ue ro nullo. De sequētibus aut̄ suo dabitur loco iudicium. In- ter omnes quos dedimus presentiatenus cabalisticos arca- norum modos, istius libri quarti progressus facilior in infi- nitū potest extendi. Quare sufficit me cupientibus amplio ra formam tradidisse simul &; causam exempli. Lumē intel ligentiae hęc facile penetrat omnia. Scripsi Peapolis, nova die Martij, Anno dn̄i M. D. Octauo. What we promised at the beginning of the third book of our work, the Polygraphia, for obtaining before the inexperienced a shadowy likeness of the new gloss, we have sufficiently fulfilled by way of example, with an abridgment of labor. We entrusted night, safely serving secrets, to be led then by shadows as a periphrasis; we have inserted numbers in the order of four lines [unclear], adapted for the use of those who wish. There are three thousand one hundred fifty places of minutiae, having fixed degrees; and, if you wish, however many moments of the hours remain are infinite, for making secret, in every nation and language of the world, whatever secret matter may occur. The circle, arising linearly from a point, as often as night exceeds the image of light, as much as you wish: if there is need, you will be able to bring it back to the path by which you came. If much of night remains, bring back the tail of the dragon to the original tail-piece in the head. But let the binary be wholly assured to us concerning the known signs of unity. He who hungers much should labor much, so that he may have something to eat. Nor is it a matter of great labor to lead whither you wish that which advances of its own accord. Here, therefore, we set an end to the third book of our Polygraphia, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Gentle reader, farewell. From Peapolium, on the seventh day of the month of March, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ our Savior 1508, in the eleventh indiction.

Here is the end of the third book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Peapolium, of the Order of Saint Benedict.

The fourth book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James the Greater, apostle, at Wurzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

[unclear]

The order of reasoning required that the fourth book of our Polygraphia be made different from the preceding ones in quality, invention, and ease, so that those wishing to share in the secrets of our matters may attain this not by one means but by various and different ones. We have extended the magpie, comprehensible by a very easy invention, so that night, always joined through the minutia to the monad in any order, may be recognized in the light of day. Here no difference is found between unity and the binary; nor will one wishing to perform the art need to have the instrument at hand, when, as the first things follow upon the last without a middle, the hidden mystery reveals itself. Hence the prudent, understanding man, experienced in the science, will at every time and place sufficiently perform the operation. The binary receives from unity, whence it produces the ternary. The first knowledge of the face of this cryptology is easy, after the moon has been illuminated by the sun, even at a single point. Yet it can also happen that an industrious gnostic may come forth without the guidance of a master. This, however, I think should be understood only in this book, but in none of the preceding ones. Concerning the following books, judgment will be given in its proper place. Among all the cabalistic methods of secrets which we have given up to the present, the procedure of this fourth book can more easily be extended to infinity. Therefore it suffices that I have handed down to those desiring more both the form and the reason of the example. The light of understanding easily penetrates all these things. I wrote at Peapolium, on the ninth day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

fatigandũ cũ iter modus praestet in infinitum, si cui ad ulteriora fuerit exemplar necessarium. Minime quoqꝫ reor necessariũ ea quae suui recitata in pręcedentibus ad memo riam reducere, cũ lector sagax si fuerit studiosus etiam que̾ in his maiora latitant possit auxiliante domino inuenire. Materiam sapienti studioso tradidimus simul causam quibus si prudenter uti voluerit, suo nostrum ingenio supe rabit. Quisquis uero hanc stratam cupit in umbra pulchri orem, ingenio manū coniungat animũ, iter sibi faciat ipse paraphrasmate pulchrius decoratum. Memoria tene¬ at fixum si quẽ ista delectant ut in orbe semper maneat pre stituto, quẽ quolibet modo praetergressius fuerit, opera tio tota inutilis euanescit. Hominũ plura sunt nomina, sunt de niqꝫ infinita pene vocabula rerum, uiiliarum, ciuitatũ, pro¬ uinciarum, herbarum, arborum, lapidum uerborũ, quae nostris omnia subseruiunt institutis. Ex his librum mo¬ dũ fieri constat nõ impossibile, si cũ diligentia sit pręsto in genium, quae nostra inuenta pręcellant in infinitum. With the demonstration of the possibility of our new invention having been shown briefly, and no less sufficiently, I do not think that I myself should be wearied any longer over the same matter on this occasion, since the method of the journey extends to infinity, if anyone should need an example for further matters. Nor do I by any means think it necessary to recall to memory the things that have been recited in the preceding sections, since a sharp reader, if he is studious, can also, with the Lord's help, discover the greater things that lie hidden in these. We have handed over the material, and at the same time the cause, to the wise student; if he wishes to use them prudently, by his own talent he will surpass ours. But whoever desires this paved road more beautiful in the shade should join hand and mind to talent, and himself make a path more beautifully adorned by paraphrase. Let him hold it fixed in memory, if these things delight anyone, that he must always remain within the prescribed circle; if he passes beyond it in any way, the whole operation vanishes uselessly. There are many names of men; indeed, there are almost infinite words for things, towns, cities, provinces, herbs, trees, stones, and verbs, all of which serve our purposes. From these it is clear that it is not impossible for a book of this kind to be made, if talent is present with diligence, which may surpass our inventions without limit. But the man of such dullness that he cannot understand these childish things of ours, when will he penetrate the subtler matters that remain? We put an end to the fourth book of the Polygraphia, to which we join the fifth in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Here is the end of the fourth book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot, on the fourteenth day of March, in the year 1508.

IOAN·TRITEMII ABBATIS SANCTI IACOBI APOSTOLI PEAPO- LITANI, POLYGRAPHIAE LIBER QVINTVS EX ORDIVM CAPIT. <Initial type="decorated-drop">E</Initial>AQVAE auxiliante domino nostro lesu Christo in quatuor praecedẽtibus li- bris pro complemento Polygraphiae nostrae utcunqꝫ digessimus, rationa- biliter exigunt, ut reliqua huiusce in- stitutionis precepta quae superfunt et amp; modos, breuiter in quinto pertractemus. Dabimur itaqꝫ modum in eo fatis compendiosum per metathesin, id est, trāspositionē literarū, quo secure, tuto, &amp; secretissime ami- cus scribet ad amicū quaecunqꝫ uoluerit. Eo scribendi mo- do Caesarē Augustū legimus usum in areanis. Qui quiđ ē nunciandi modus et amp; si multipliciter sit securus, semꝑ tn̄ in- tuentibus habetur suspectus: quia mox ut literarū cernitur trāspositio, qui curiosus est aliquid sub eis latere protinus suspicatur. Sunt aūt modi huius adinuentionis pene infini- ti, e quibus nos pro necessaria introductione sequentes le- ctori praesignauimus, cuius reliqua ingenio ꝑscrutanda re- feruamus. In primis ergo tabulā huius industriae p̃misimꝰ canonicā, cui altera subiecinus auersam. In his duabus ta- bulis radix et amp; fundamentū memorate trāspositionis omni- no ponit᷑, sup quo structura totius aedificij collocatur. His etem̃ duabus tabulis rite cognitis et amp; intellectis, nulla trans- positio literarū latere poterit cũ diligētia operantē. His qͣ tuor et amp; uiginti alphabetę ꝑ ordinē cōiunximus, ut lectori copiā transponēdi grāmata p̄beremus. Horū usus pro uo- to cōsistit in singulis, aut si malueris etiā in uniuerfis. Sitibi- cū multis fuerit arcani cōmertiū, alphabeta singula famili- aribus tuis distribue singulis, tu uero memoriae cōmanda</Line> <Gap reason="damaged" extent="ca. 1 char"/> quid unicuiqꝫ tradideris Primo quidē alphabetū cōmittatur primū secundo secundum: tertio tertiū, & ita consequēter fiat de reliquis Quod si prae multitudine negociorū autfamiliae alphabeta qua e signauimus nō sufficerēt ad oīa uelsi aliq̄ ex eis nimisuideant patula manifesta, uarias trāspositiones nouas poterimus inducere, quarū numerusfit maximus, arcani modus ꝑpetuo maneat semp occultus.Cuius rei ponamus exemplū: B fit a,f sit b,l litér,p sitd,t site,z sit f,e sit g,m sith, ita consequenter per totū alphabetū usuale fiat ut inter quālibet literā assumptā tres ineriaceant ociose atqꝫ transposite.Postea quatuor, deiindequinqꝫ plures aut pauciores,ita tn̄ q̃totū alphabetū quasitreuolutū in orbēconcurrat, litera nulla penitus obmittatur,sed unaquaeqꝫeadē serie pro alia in ordine suo collocetur.Qualicūqꝫmodo scripseris ipsum aut litteris aut memoriae tenaciter noueris cōmendandū, ne p obligiuonēlapsus,quod scripleras ipse legere iā nō possis. Tot em̄ modis litetrarumtranspositioruariaripotest, quod secundū estimationē intellectus humani ꝗ operarione temporali cōclususin corpore mortali nō capit proprie infinita, mortalis consurget numerus innumerabilis.Vnde quicūqꝫmodos scrībendi per metathesin plures habere uoluerit a nostrainstitutione remotos,si uel parum fuerit ingeniosus diligens,facilē in operatione sua cōsequetur effectū.Maximaenim potest ingeniū hominis si studio īuuetur arte.Quiaūt spernit minima,nunq̃ pertinget ad maiora.Scio pleroscqꝫ futuros qui haec studia nostrauatuana puerilia deridehunt,quibus damus pro responso.nos omnino fore cōtentos modo illis cōplaceant,ad quorum sunt instantiam abiscomposita.Sequitur tabula recta.

The fifth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James the Apostle at Würzburg, begins its preface.

Those things which, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have arranged, however imperfectly, in the four preceding books for the completion of our Polygraphy, reasonably require that in the fifth book we briefly treat the remaining precepts and methods of this instruction which are left over. We shall therefore give in it a sufficiently concise method by metathesis, that is, the transposition of letters, by which a friend may safely, securely, and most secretly write to a friend whatever he wishes. We read that Caesar Augustus used this method of writing in secret matters. Although this method of communication is in many ways secure, nevertheless it is always regarded with suspicion by those who inspect it, because as soon as a transposition of letters is perceived, anyone who is curious at once suspects that something lies hidden beneath them.

There are, moreover, almost infinite methods of this invention; from these, for the necessary introduction, we have set out the following for the reader, reserving the rest to be investigated by his ingenuity. First, therefore, we have placed before him the canonical table of this craft, to which we have joined another, reversed. In these two tables the root and foundation of the aforementioned transposition is wholly set down, upon which the structure of the entire edifice is placed. For when these two tables have been properly known and understood, no transposition of letters will be able to remain hidden from one who works diligently. To these we have joined twenty-four alphabets in order, so that we might provide the reader with an abundance of ways of transposing letters. The use of these, according to one’s wish, consists in individual alphabets, or, if you prefer, also in all of them. If you have a secret correspondence with many people, distribute individual alphabets to individual acquaintances, but commit to memory what you have given to each one [unclear].

Let the first alphabet be entrusted to the first, the second to the second, the third to the third, and so let it be done consequently with the rest. But if, because of the multitude of affairs or of one’s household, the alphabets which we have marked out should not suffice for everything, or if some of them seem too open and manifest, we shall be able to introduce various new transpositions, whose number becomes very great, while the method of the secret always remains perpetually hidden. Let us give an example of this matter: let B be a, F be b, L be c, P be d, T be e, Z be f, E be g, M be h; let it be done thus consecutively through the whole usual alphabet, so that between any assumed letter three letters intervene idly and in transposed order. Afterward four, then five, more or fewer; yet so that the whole alphabet, as though revolved in a circle, comes together, no letter at all is omitted, but each one is placed in the same series for another in its own order.

In whatever way you write, you must know that the method itself is to be committed firmly either to letters or to memory, lest, having slipped through forgetfulness, you can no longer read what you yourself had written. For the transposition of letters can be varied in so many ways that, according to the estimation of human understanding, which, enclosed by temporal operation in a mortal body, does not properly grasp infinite things, an innumerable number will arise for a mortal man. Hence whoever wishes to have more methods of writing by metathesis, apart from our instruction, will easily achieve the result in his work if he is even a little ingenious and diligent. For the human intellect can accomplish very great things if it is aided by study and art. But he who despises small things will never attain to greater ones.

I know that there will be many who will mock these pursuits of ours as empty and childish; to them we give as an answer that we shall be altogether content provided they please those at whose urging they have been composed by us. The direct table follows.

Straight table of transposition.

[letter table]

In this canonical, or straight, table of letters, from our single usual alphabet of the Latin letters themselves, by change or transposition, you have as many alphabets as there are monograms in it throughout, namely twenty-four times twenty-four, which make in number 576; and multiplied again by the same number, they make a little less than fourteen thousand.

Table of reversed transposition.

[letter table]

In this second reversed table you have as many alphabets by transposition of letters as we also set down in the preceding straight one. For, as you see, under metathesis there are twenty-four toward the right; likewise as many toward the left; twenty-four downward, and twenty-four upward. These, multiplied by ninety-eight twenty-four times and reduced in the form of a cross to the four sides, make not fewer than 112 alphabets.

The same table expanded follows.

In the second alphabet c is taken for a, in the third d, in the fourth e, in the fifth f, as the placement of the order shows.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot [unclear], sends greetings to the reader.

Since all the letters of the Greeks and the Hebrews are numerical, I have often wondered that the painstaking Latinity of the ancients did not also make its own letters serve the reckoning of numbers. The Hebrews, by a duplication of certain letters, established twenty-eight signs sufficient for every number. The Greeks, however, remedied this lack of letters with like foresight by adding four characters. Therefore, since we have twenty-four letters, why should we not also make ours numerical, since we can similarly find four to be duplicated? Let us give four as an example, and it will be quite enough for every number: m and final nj; likewise long s and final or closed s; likewise closed v and open u. When we add these to the twenty-four usual letters, we have twenty-eight characters sufficient for all numbers. Nor will it be a matter of great labor to grasp this method of numbering for those who already know letters, if once they commit it to memory.

For this invention of ours may be useful to many, since with few letters it comprises many thousands in number, all of which can be distinguished and understood at first sight, without any calculation, more clearly than by the figures of algorism, especially in large numbers, as seems to many who are less experienced in the art of calculation not to be possible so easily. For as soon as you have looked with your eye upon a number, however large, you will be able both fully to understand it and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. Since this is easy, it is fitting that we set down the letters themselves reduced to number. I wrote this on 16 March, in the year 1509.

[unclear]

Behold, reader, you have the method by which you can sufficiently mark and write every writable number with a few letters; their extension, as you see, proceeds to infinity. But, as it was once customary to say in a proverb, “A weary ox plants his foot firmly.” Whoever wishes to be content with former things should follow the ancient method of numbering. So that those who do not know it may understand it more easily, it will not be tedious for me to give in what follows the form which Hunibald, the historian of the Franks, and also Bede, Rabanus, Helpericus the monks, and many of the ancients used in chronicles and ecclesiastical calculations, as follows.

NDS IOAN•TRITEMII ABBATIS SANCTI IACOBI MAIORIS APOSTO LI HERBIPOLENSIS LIBER POLYGRAPHIAE SEXTVS INITIVM SVMIT. <Initial type="decorated-drop">A</Initial>NTESOMNEM inuentionē et amp; usum literarū in primordio mundi cum homines adhuc ru- des essent ingenio moribus inculti, sub tri- um cōmunicatiōe uicissitudinis regimine, ut quidā opinantur intelligentiarum per annos mille sexaginta tres sibi per ordinē succeden tes, erat̃ in orbe planetarū influentiae corporibus in terra suo mo do praestantes. Dicunt huius rei speculatores antiqui saturnū a mudi principio germinatis in terra nascentibus praefuisse influe- do principaliter sua moderante intelligentia, quā orificelem, hoc est, uiufificantē dei nuncuparunt, annis lunaribus trecentis quin¬ quaginta quatuor, mensib us item quatuor, ac diebus horisqꝫ to tidem. Quae nos ut poetica recensemus, nō confirmamus. Post sa turnū Venus, post Venerem Iupiter dominiū ponitur assumpsis¬ se. Post Iouem uero mercurius in ordine quartus, dominator in genia hominum diuersis artibus decorauit. We have hitherto set forth, for example's sake, the manner of writing numbers by Latin letters [used by] the ancient Franks of Germany, that we might offer the knowledge of it also to those who do not know [it]. But that, in the placing of the figures of the algorism, we have departed from the common rule of computation, was done not from error but from a reasonable cause—namely, lest we be burdened in too great a progression. There were also [those] who wrote larger numbers in such a manner. [a third numeral table; partly garbled.]

These [matters] concerning the reckoning of numbers being duly completed, we end also the fifth book of Polygraphy. In the year of the Lord 1508.

Before every invention and use of letters, in the beginning of the world, when men were still rude in talent [and] uncultivated in morals—under the rule of the alternating communication of the three [intelligences], as some suppose, the intelligences succeeding one another in order through one thousand and sixty-three years—the influences of the planets were present in the world, in their own manner excelling [over] bodies on earth. The ancient speculators of this matter say that Saturn, from the beginning of the world, presided over the [things] germinating [and] being born on earth, by influence, his intelligence principally moderating [it]—which intelligence they named Orifiel, that is, the life-giving [intelligence] of God—for three hundred and fifty-four lunar years, four months, and as many days and hours. These [things] we recount as poetical, [and] do not confirm. After Saturn, Venus; after Venus, Jupiter is set down to have assumed the dominion. But after Jupiter, Mercury, fourth in order, as ruler, adorned the talents of men with diverse arts. But under the three intelligences mentioned—Saturn, namely, Venus, and Jupiter—ruling, they assert that men had not even the knowledge of letters. Whence, as often as one wished to announce something secret to another, he did this not by writings—since the office of letters was lacking—but by certain similitudes of animals, trees, plants, or of other sensible [things], symbolically, according as each had agreed among themselves. The time of Saturn gave to men, as they say, morals properly agreeing with [his] influence. For it made [them] farmers, hunters, founders of cities, rude, wild, sad, simple, uncultivated in life [and] morals, living long in the flesh. After Orifiel of Saturn, as those so opining [say], they say the intelligence Anael, the mover of Venus, [received] the governance of the world by influence, taking three hundred and fifty-four years…

[unclear], months, days, and four hours; under him men began to be more cultivated, to build houses more frequently, and cities, and also to invent various manual arts, namely the work of weaving, wool-working, and many other things similar to these. They also began to sink more deeply into the pleasures of the flesh, and, taking beautiful wives, with many children begotten from them, they fell notably away from natural simplicity. They invented games and songs; they began to play the cithara; whatever they maintained pertained to the influence of Venus, they devised with greater zeal, following too much the motion of the flesh.

They called the third intelligence of Jupiter Zachariel; receiving the dominion of the world after Anael, it made men restless with desire for rule, to go hunting, to make tents, to adorn themselves with various garments. While he held dominion, in accordance with the quality of Jupiter, who deprived his father of the kingdom, there arose a great division between the good and the wicked: the former invoking God, the latter given over to the flesh and the world. Under that rule Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all posterity the testament of dying once.

But the fourth mover, or angel, of Mercury, Raphael, influencing worldly things after Zachariel, began in the one thousand fifty-fifth year of the world, at the end of the month of February, and lasted until the one thousand four hundred tenth year of the world; under him the use of letters is said first to have been invented. The letters then, however, as they report, were different from those which the world has today, devised in the form and likeness of trees, plants, and animals; yet with time these were afterward altered in many ways, and took on an easier and more cultivated manner of being formed. For the fictions of the poets said that Mercury was the patron of all literature, promising that great hidden mysteries of things lay beneath their fables.

After this, when the human race had multiplied and had been spread everywhere over the whole earth, the unity of letters did not long remain; but the separation of bodies and minds far from one another discovered different and various modes of writing, concerning which a long narration would be needed from us. Plato the philosopher, in the Phaedrus, relates that a certain philosopher named Theotones first invented letters and the use of writing, together with the system of weights, numbers, and the game of dice, and taught Thamus, king of the Egyptians.

Concerning the rest, however, and the ancient men who are said to have handed down special letters to almost individual nations and peoples, which remain in use among them down to the present day, it is not my purpose on this occasion to set out or describe a narrative. For all our learned men know that Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians, is said first to have brought sixteen letters into Greece: αβγδεζθκλμνοπρστυφψχω. [unclear] ε, κ, ω, λ, μ, β, ζ, σ, τ, ψ. To these Palamedes, at the time of the Trojan War, is reported to have added four: [unclear], θ, φ, χ. And afterward Pythagoras added the letter v, so that there should be twenty-one; and κ and ϖ were subsequently invented by others. Gordanis, bishop of the Goths, gave his people letters proper to them. When the unity of language had been confounded, the simplicity of characters was also varied in many ways. From this it happened that the use of letters, in the course of time, claimed such license for itself that not only individual peoples, but also individual men, fashioning new characters for letters at their own judgment, prepared hiding places for their mysteries.

Yet every writing in unusual characters will not be free from suspicion on the part of those who see it. Notwithstanding this, many kings, tyrants, and princes of old devised for themselves a private mode of writing, separated from the common one, caring little for the suspicion of others, provided that what they wished to remain secret was not perceived. Moved by imitation of them, and wishing to bring to a perfect end this work of the Polygraphia, so far as can be done, in this sixth book, which is also the last, I have determined to call back from the dead certain characters of the ancients which have long since ceased from mortal use, lest they perish utterly. And first indeed we shall set down the ancient manner of writing of the Northmen.

are referred to, namely c, d, i, l, m, v, and so forth. The Northmen, however, together with the Asiatic Dacians, having once come forth from the Scandinavian islands, which are now called Gothic, roamed through Gaul for more than forty years and devastated it most severely. In order to provide for their secret affairs, as Bede, the English monk, testifies, they devised from the letters of the Greeks the following new and handsome manner of writing. For they adapted the numerals of the Greeks, comprised in ten letters up to twenty-four, to Latin characters, and under a foreign form prudently concealed our letters, namely in the way in which we use numbers in place of letters: that is, for a we put 1, for b, 2, for c, 3, for d, 4, and so in sequence to the end of the alphabet. A handsome invention indeed, and sufficiently secure, which neither a Greek nor a Latin will easily understand. For the whole alphabet is not found in it, but only nine letters, and one numerical sign, namely g, which among them signifies six, and in this manner of writing f, the sixth letter of the Latins. Moreover, deferring to our German language, in which we were born, we have placed at the end the double w as the twenty-fourth letter of our nation, which, according to the Greek numeral, we formed thus: ꝟ. This writing of the Northmen, then, let us set down from the following order of Greek letters, in imitation of them.

represent Latin letters, and they cannot be read either by a Greek or by a Latin who has not previously acquired knowledge of this device. This manner of writing can also be varied in many ways, when the letters are changed by transposition of the number. This can be done in the full Greek letters according to the wish and judgment of any industrious writer. Nor will the method of forming these characters be very difficult, especially for one who has had a little practice. The characters written above are also sufficiently suited to the German language, since with them we can denote all things that occur to us, in whatever speech we are skilled. Whenever iota is placed by itself, so that it may be known to denote the letter k, the tenth of the alphabet, it is marked above thus: ī.

Concerning the Alphabet and Method of Writing of the Ancient Franks.

[unclear]

The opinion of very many holds that the Germans once had letters from the Greeks, and they affirm firmly that they used the Greek language, especially in their sacred rites. For they say that there is a great consonance between the Greek language and our own, although the long interval of time has utterly extinguished that agreement. That most learned man, once my teacher, Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, most reverend bishop of the church of Worms, had collected some thousands of Greek words which have the same meaning in both languages, Greek and German. And Caesar testifies in his Commentaries that the ancient Druids, the priests of sacred rites in Gaul, used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. But when the Romans were devastating the world, they at length violently imposed the use of their own letters, together with their dominion, upon many nations. in the [unclear]-fortieth, having gone out from the borders of the Scythians, with King Marcomer furnishing leadership, they came into Germany, and received settlements from their Saxon brothers at the mouths of the Rhine. Thereafter, for nine hundred and fifty years, waging almost continual war with the Romans and Gauls, as Hunibald is the authority, they finally subjected almost all Europe to their command or kingdom. Yet, once they had received the letters of the Romans, they did not destroy them, but rather, being themselves mingled among the Germans and Gauls, they learned their language, and preserved their letters and the form of their writings. Vuasthaldus, a writer of the histories of this people, wrote books in his native speech on the deeds of kings, dukes, and princes over nearly seven hundred and fifty-eight years, with the characters appended, as Hunibald says, which he mentions in his volume that he published in eighteen books on the origin of the Franks.

Unless the fault of the scribe has deceived me, I have, as I think, suitably reproduced the alphabet of Wasthaldus; in it some characters differ entirely from the Greek, while some also seem partly to resemble them. Yet I do not know what I should judge: whoever their inventor may have been, although he did not preserve the form of the Greek letters, he nevertheless observed the order of the letters. The codex, falling apart from excessive age, could scarcely be read; hence I fear that I have rather been deceived by some interpolator than found the true and certain opinion of Hunibald.

But let us pass on to the things that remain, since if Hunibald's statement is true, it will have been well written by us; but if it is someone's fiction, it will neither harm us nor do injury to the reader. Another fictitious alphabet follows, found in the codex of Hunibald, to which this was inscribed:

The alphabet of the Franks, which Doracus invented.

Whoever wishes to use the characters written above should know that they are to be written beneath the lines, in the manner of the Greeks, not above as the Latins do. Likewise it must be observed that, of the double letters, the first are written at the beginning and in the middle of words, but the second always at the end.

From the grammarians of Otfridus, monk of Wissembourg.

We have read that Charles, king of the Franks, surnamed the Great, taking pity on the barbarism of his nation, with Nanno, Theobald, Albinus, and Berenger as helpers, attempted to bring the German language under rule. And although, as Turpin bears witness, he had begun so arduous a work, he did not complete it, being delayed by frequent incursions of wars, but, overtaken by death, left it unfinished; nor did another arise after him who would recall concern for this matter to his mind. But Otfridus, the aforesaid monk, formerly hearer and disciple of Rabanus Fuldaensis, under Louis the Pious, son of that Charles, having mastered that grammar, albeit imperfectly, wrote many things in our German language, which seem to sound with a remarkable weight of regular instruction, in meter both grave and elegiac; moreover he also composed some things in prose to Louis, king of Germany, son of Louis the Pious and brother of the emperor Lothar; also to Orgarius, archbishop of Mainz, to the monks of Saint Gall, and to others. Having obtained fragments of this grammar, I too have extracted the present characters of the alphabet from many, lest they utterly perish. Moreover it is established, on Otfridus' testimony, that Charles devised several alphabets of his own, by which he could safely use his very broad kingdom in secret matters with the individual prefects. From these, with Otfridus supplying them, we commit a few things to these letters.

Charles, the great king and most Christian emperor, fought with the Saxons for not less than thirty years; finally overcoming them by the sword, he converted them to the Christian faith. But fearing lest they should again apostatize from the faith, as they had done many times, he appointed certain secret investigators, to whom he granted judicial power, who, traveling through all Saxony, should secretly and diligently inquire concerning the faith and morals of the people; and whoever they found to have apostatized from the faith, robbers, adulterers, blasphemers, despisers of the church or of its priests and commands, or [those guilty] of notorious crimes against the Christian

disturbing the public [peace?], or recalling or soliciting the people to paganism, they were, without delay, by imperial and royal authority and with impunity, to hang with a noose or otherwise kill as they could. But so that this institution might remain forever unshaken, he gave the same men power to substitute also others, fit under certain conditions, who, enjoying the aforesaid faculty, might with impunity exercise the office of inquisition and death against the guilty. Finally he prescribed for them secret laws, hidden signs, and also the form of an oath, by which they might proceed justly in judging and punishing, and, known to one another, might remain hidden from others, and might forever preserve the necessary, more secret tribunal in Saxon land. They also used certain alphabets among themselves for a time, which nevertheless in the end fell wholly out of use. Yet the office of an inquisition of this kind remains down to the present time, whose ministers are commonly called Feimers.

If anyone according to his own judgment wishes to devise a new alphabet for himself, he should know that two things in particular must be observed, which, however, I do not always find [observed?] in the foregoing. The first is that he form characters easy to draw; and the simpler they are, the better they will be. The second is that he arrange the individual letters so that, joined into words, they present a beautiful and elegant appearance. I add a third, not promised: if you wish the writing to remain secret, make some letters of the alphabet double, after the manner of the Hebrews.

This Frank [Hicbus?] came with Marcomer from the borders of Scythia to the mouths of the Rhine in Germany, and is said to have invented these characters as a supplement to the German language; they seem to agree with it fairly well in many respects. From Latin letters also manifold alphabets are made, when, either reduced to number according to the pattern that we handed down in the preceding fifth book, or otherwise, in imitation of the Northmen, together also with Greek letters, they furnish us a very secure method of announcing whatever we wish. Let us accordingly set the letters themselves, unusually changed, according to the number and order of our customary alphabet, and we shall have a secret and mystical method of writing, quite beautiful and elegant, confirmed by practice. This method of numbering, however, is different from that which we placed in the fifth book, and more suitable to our purpose.

Alchemy has many domestic handmaids and familiars, who guard their mistress with perpetual vigilance, and put themselves forward in her name, so that they may preserve her from intercourse with so many importunate lovers, untouched for all time. Vanity, fraud, deceitfulness, deception, sophification, greed, falsity, lying confidence, stupidity, want, poverty, despair, flight, proscription, and beggary are the attendants of alchemy, who, pretending to be the beloved mistress, keep her inviolate, and gladly offer themselves in her place to her moneyed, avaricious, greedy, and foolish seekers.

On the signs and wonderful but excessively laborious method of writing of M. T. Cicero, and afterward of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr.

Marcus Tullius Cicero, the eloquent orator of the Romans, wrote a book of signs of no small size, which Saint Cyprian, prelate of the Carthaginians, martyr, enlarged with many signs and words, adding vocabulary necessary for Christian uses, so that the work itself became not only more [unclear], but also [unclear] for the faithful.

The codex is rare, found by me only once, and bought at a cheap price. For in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1496, when for love of books I was inspecting several libraries, I found the aforesaid codex in a certain monastery of our order, neglected through excessive age, cast away under dust and despised. I asked the abbot, a doctor of law, at what value he held it. He replied that he would prefer to it the little works of Saint Anselm, recently printed. I went to the booksellers, since the matter happened in a metropolitan city; I bought the requested little works of Anselm for a sixth part of a florin, gave them to the abbot and the rejoicing monks, and rescued the codex, already brought nearly to destruction. For, out of love of parchment, they had resolved that it should immediately be scraped.

Almost two years after this, when I went up to Strasbourg on business of my order, and was admitted by Johann Geiler of Kaysersberg, the distinguished preacher of the place, into the library of the greater church, I found a whole psalter written out in these same signs of Tullius and Cyprian, most fittingly written in gold at the head. But the title had been placed outside thus by someone ignorant of the mystery: “Psalter in the Armenian language.” I brought in a learned man, showed the falsity, and advised that it be retitled: “Psalter written in Ciceronian signs.” Whether he did so or not I am uncertain, since afterward I did not return to that library. That you may see, reader, the form of Cicero’s notation, we have determined to append a few signs.

[Table of signs and equivalents, partly unclear:]

Vii = approves; W = modest; L = letter. 2i = approves; h = immodest; b = letter. 10 = wicked; M = moderate; g = syllable. 3 = upright; In = immoderate; k = time. A = uprightness; M = accommodating; t = [unclear]. B = wickedness; m = inconvenient; s = [unclear]. C = probable; T = accommodates; u = temporal. D = disapproves; S = beyond measure; v = extra-temporal. M = measure; H = in what way; y = man.

You need, indeed, a great memory for the method of writing, and an entirely immense labor of reading, where any character either signifies an entire word, or a final syllable, or some part of speech suitable for the composition of the whole. Therefore, all the signs being omitted, let us draw out an alphabet from a few.

[Alphabet of signs: unclear characters preserved in the Latin source.]

Many other new alphabets could also be formed from Cicero’s signs; we leave the drawing-out of them to the judgment of anyone who wishes to do it. For the book is very full, and contains many signs, notably differing from one another, all of which serve writers.

[Greek-letter alphabet.]

This was the alphabet of Iaimiclis, the great king of the [Articori?], surnamed Megalopius, a very wise man, which he used in secret matters; it too can be changed in many ways. To this, out of love for our prince, we have appended the following, in which, if it is more often used over time, writing will become easier.

[Greek-letter alphabet.]

How also by numbers and in many other various ways we can safely write any secrets whatever.

These things are childish, I admit, since everyone according to his own capacity and judgment can devise more numerous and more elegant alphabets than we have recorded in this volume. Therefore we knowingly omit many things which in a similar way are childish, common, and [unclear].

We judge it to be of little usefulness. We fear that someday we shall be ashamed to have turned our mind to these trifles, more useful matters having been set aside. But I pray that readers will spare me, since my own will did indeed draw me back from these childish studies, not to say at least partly vain ones; but the insistence of certain friends compelled me to write them, and indeed I could not refuse them this without injury to the bond of obligation contracted. Nevertheless, induced by their entreaty, I also had to connect the following chapter with the preceding matters, and to assign numbers for letters. For the ancients arranged various and manifold methods of writing under the figures of numbers, by which, through subtle invention, they safely transmitted their secrets to one another. Therefore, persuaded by the prayers of friends, we have placed a few methods out of many at the end of this sixth book, by which a path to knowledge of the others may lie open to those who do not know them. For if anyone delights to know these things, once these are known he will easily be able to ascend to higher matters, and to vary the methods discovered with manifold interchange at his own discretion. As the beginning of this matter, we have placed a table under the orchema, which, when the reading is varied in the manner of a cross, will contain ninety-six alphabets in itself.

We do not expand the orchemata, being moved by a rational cause, because, since it ranges more widely in its progression, the immense labor has frightened the mind. We have also deliberately passed over unity, not assigning it a place; to set it before our inventions in due order we judge rash. For from those things which we have already shown by way of example, anyone who is fit in understanding will easily attain greater things. All things serve secrets.

prae- monemus. Primo, ut quotiés alphabeto uitit̃ cuiusdĕ prudenter apponat, ge- mine utilitatis gratia. Per hoc enim nimius labor aufertur ami- co lectori, &amp; manebit in secreto mysteriũ, dū industriae quicũ¬ ꝗignarus, tabulã numeris scriptã et amp; signoꝵ uel planetarũ cha- racteribus praenotata ad Astronomiae ratione pertinere puta bit, &amp; nihil penitus mysterij latere suspicabitur. Nā ea de cau¬ sa nō ab unitate materiã officialẽ literis, sed a distante suscepti¬ mus, ne suspicionis notã aliqͥui praeberemus. Prudẽtia nihilo minus adhibenda est scriptoribus, quoniã lector astutus qui de suspicione latẽtis tangitur, si officiũ unius numeri deprehẽ derit, totũ alphabetũ facile supputabit. Secundo memēto quis quis huius rei cupis esse sagax operator, ut quotiens in dictio ne qualibet littera geminatur, ut saepius fit, non scribatur nisi se mel et amp; superius puncto notetur. Vt exempli gratia, uolo de al¬ phabeto arietis serbere Ioannes, non duplico 18. quod est n, sed scribo sic, 14. 19. 6. 13. 10. 23. uel abbas. 6 ꝗ̈. 6. 23. ioanes, abas, ut omnis nota suspensionis auferatur. In similibus cautela est si¬ mili agendũ, quia nisi operator sit industriâ preditus, nouerit ꝗ ex paruis inuenire maiora, nō erit idoneus cui haec minima nosterà debeant aperiiri. Latent in singulis passibus</Initial>

In this figure we have placed, for each of the remaining six signs, individual alphabets by numbers, just as they are seen set beneath the Latin letters in order, so that anyone who wishes may more safely conceal his secrets by means of them.

We have, by God’s mercy, brought the sixth and last book of our Polygraphy to its close; in it, ending our discourse with the wandering stars, we give the reader advance warning on certain points.

First, whenever he uses the alphabet of any given [sign?], he should prudently attach it, for the sake of a double advantage. For by this excessive labor is removed from the friendly reader, and the secret will remain hidden, since anyone ignorant of the craft will suppose that a table written with numbers and marked beforehand with the characters of signs or planets pertains to the reckoning of astronomy, and will not at all suspect that any secret lies hidden. For that reason we have not taken up the official matter of the letters from unity, but from a distance, lest we give anyone any mark of suspicion. Nevertheless prudence must be used by writers, since a clever reader who is touched by suspicion of something hidden, if he discovers the function of one number, will easily calculate the whole alphabet.

Second, let anyone who desires to be a shrewd practitioner of this matter remember that whenever a letter is doubled in any word, as often happens, it should be written only once and marked above with a point. For example, I wish to write Ioannes from the alphabet of Aries: I do not double 18, which is n, but I write thus: 14. 19. 6. 13. 10. 23.; or abbas: 6 [unclear]. 6. 23.; Ioanes, abas, so that every mark of suspension may be removed. In similar cases, similar caution must be employed; for unless the practitioner is endowed with diligence and knows how to find greater things from small ones, he will not be fit to have these least things of ours disclosed to him.

Not all things are to be communicated indiscriminately to everyone, especially those whose use can be turned to good and evil. Moved reasonably by that consideration, we have plainly handed down many things in these six books of the Polygraphy to those wishing to know, but we have allowed far more secrets to lie hidden beneath manifest things. Finally, we have written out a key that unfolds the whole work, explaining how each metaphor is to be understood; nevertheless, by the advice of certain persons, we have ordered it to remain hidden at home, so that students may not lack material for exercising their memory, and the wicked may be deprived of the means of knowing those things which they are not willing to use well. There lie hidden in each step

...more mysteries; and the greater things you find from these, the greater things remain to be found. A way is prepared for beginners, in which, as they advance, it will not be difficult in the course of time to find many things, both rare and very great. Here one who did not know how will learn to write in Latin, and prudently to wrap all the mysteries of his will in a foreign speech. But that an unlearned man may be able to understand not only his own mysteries which he wraps up, but also open speech, of which until now he has always been ignorant, is a matter of no great labor, if the paraphrast has fully attained our intention in this volume. For beneath the bark lie hidden the kernels of our Steganographia, buried for good reason, lest they lie open to unworthy babblers. Finally, it had been worth the effort that one work should not prejudice the other, but that its own right should be distributed inviolate to each. Wearied after a long voyage, we here cast anchor in the deep under the name of JESUS CHRIST, savior of the faithful, on the twenty-first day of the month of March, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1508, in the eleventh Roman indiction, at Paeapolis, the city of the East Franks, which they also call Würzburg and Herbipolis.

Here is the end of the sixth book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot at St. James in Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict.

Johannes Trithemius.

Preface to the Explanation of the Whole Work of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Paeopolis, that is, Würzburg, at St. James.

No one who has read these things, as I trust, will judge me either proud or superfluous, because I myself have commented on the Polygraphia recently composed by me, especially if he has been able to weigh precisely what cause induced us to speak obscurely. For whatever can do harm when made public had reasonably to be hidden in mystical speech. But the subject which we treat in the Polygraphia is, for the advantage of the commonwealth among good men, very good, useful, and honorable; and for this reason, persuaded by a reasonable cause, we wrote it, so that by its service we might render good men safe and secure from the investigation of the wicked in communicating their secrets to one another. But lest an occasion of deceiving the simpler and less cautious in their judgment of things be offered to wicked and perverse men, who very often abuse even the inventions of the good, we handed down in it mystical or hidden modes of writing, and covered the truth hidden in the marrow with certain coverings of figures. Yet we do not in the least doubt that any industrious man, desirous of these things, will easily grasp everything, if he applies even moderate perseverance in searching them out. For the things I have handed down are neither so difficult nor wrapped in such great mysteries that they cannot be thoroughly penetrated by a studious man. For everywhere we have so tempered the enigmas of our words that they may easily be passable to learned and studious men, while nevertheless remaining inaccessible to lazy men of darkness. But after it pleased us to offer the work of the Polygraphia itself, dedicated, to the most serene and unconquered Caesar of the Romans, Maximilian, ever august emperor of the world, I judged that it would be worthwhile if I made it clear with brief and few interpretations.

Expositio in prologum. <Initial type="decorated-drop">C</Initial>MNIS intentio nostra in toto polygraphiae opere circa eã uersatur sententiam, qua mo- dos traderemus certos occulte scribendi, ꝑ quos reges et amp; principes, nobiles et amp; igno- bles, sacerdotes et amp; laici, docti simul et amp; indocti, secrete, tuto, &amp; sine ulla suspitione la- tentis arcani, sibi mutuo et amp; quibuslibet amicis, etiã longe abin- uicẽ distantibus, ministerio literarũ quiquid et amp; quotiens opus fuerit mentiũ suarum queant nunciare cõceptũ. Quodne uel pri mi uel soli pręsumpsisse uideamur praemonemus lectorẽ plures olim ueterum, maxime tyrannos, principes et amp; reges simili cõsy deratiõe motos, familiares sibi ac uarios excogitauisse mõs et amp; canones scribēdi, quibus id quod uniuersaliter in polygraphia nostra sumus polliciti, particulariter ipsi tentauerunt. E quo rũ numero primũ introduximus exempli causa propositi Caesarẽ Augustum, cuius occultũ scribendi modum sic accipe manife- stū. Spiramina uocis cōceptae ex lucidis mutauit ī opaca, quoꝝ barbariē uotis renītentẽ, pulchra quadē adinuētiōe metathese os orchemate, cōuenientē ad nutũ efficit. Hoc ẽ, Magnus coefar Augustus quo secrete ac tuto scriberet qđ uoluit, alphabeti li teras uaria trāspositiōe mutauit, ita ut poneret b. pro a. c. pro b. &; fic cōsequēter de singulis. Et quo scriptura magis tortuosa ma neret secretior, pro suo arbitrio literas trāsposuit in latű &; longū ad quālibet ordinis nūeri &; loci distantiã. Mysteriũ. Et istere ceptiuus ordo ꝙͣsi p̄petuus thelemati tēporisqƺ rōi subiectus, ꝙͥuis nuncios ab incursiōe bacuceoꝝ in uia tutos cōferuet, metas tn̄ nõ habes regulatas, oës sibi occurrētes de suspicione rei latē tis facit sollicitos. Licet nemo queat mysteriũ ar canū latẽs sub trāspositione literarũ facile ad intellectũ comprehendere, facit tn̄ eos haec scriptura in quoꝝ puenerit manus de latibulo rei introclusę suspitiosos. and plain, lest the mind of the sacred Majesty, which is daily stretched by many affairs and cares, be drawn away from the understanding of it by the obscurity of mysteries. For, unless my opinion deceives me, the work will be the more welcome and useful to his Majesty the briefer and clearer it is. First, therefore, by the Lord’s bounty, we shall briefly explain the meaning of our purpose, which is contained in the prologue wrapped in various riddles; then, through the individual books of the Polygraphy, we shall set forth succinctly, to the powers of our talent, the modes of working, the rules, cautions, and individual differences, in order, as far as remains necessary.

All these things, so that they may the more quickly become accessible to those who desire to know them, we shall show in sequence by examples, and we shall be as brief as the subject and reason permit.

Key to the Explanation of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of [Peapolis?].

Exposition on the Prologue.

Our whole intention in the entire work of the Polygraphy turns upon this purpose: that we should hand down certain methods of writing secretly, by which kings and princes, nobles and commoners, priests and laymen, learned and unlearned alike, may secretly, safely, and without any suspicion of a hidden secret, by the service of letters, announce to one another and to any friends, even those at a great distance from one another, whatever conception of their minds may be needed, and as often as needed. And lest we seem to have attempted this either first or alone, we forewarn the reader that many of the ancients long ago, especially tyrants, princes, and kings, moved by similar consideration, devised for themselves familiar and various methods and rules of writing, by which they themselves attempted in particular what we have promised universally in our Polygraphy. From their number, for the sake of an example of the proposed matter, we first introduced Caesar Augustus, whose hidden mode of writing take as plainly thus.

He changed the breathings of the conceived voice from clear signs into obscure ones; by a certain fine invention of metathesis, by [unclear], he makes their barbarousness, though resisting the vows, conform to his command. That is: the great Caesar Augustus, so that he might write secretly and safely what he wished, changed the letters of the alphabet by varied transposition, so that he put b for a, c for b, and so consequently with each one. And so that the writing, being more twisted, might remain more secret, he transposed the letters at his pleasure sideways and lengthwise to whatever distance of order, number, and place.

Mystery. And that deceptive order, as though perpetual, subject to the will and to the reckoning of time, although it keeps messengers safe on the road from the assault of [unclear], nevertheless, since it has no regulated limits, makes all who meet them anxious with suspicion of a hidden matter.

Explanation. Although no one can easily comprehend with the understanding the hidden mystery lying beneath the transposition of the letters, nevertheless this writing makes those into whose hands it comes suspicious about the hiding-place of the matter enclosed within.

Mystery. That Archimedes of Syracuse, easily the foremost of mathematicians, made a white bird, suitable to his instructions, naked by head and feet, and the rest.

Explanation. Archimedes had two little rods of one length and thickness planed, round or square, of which he kept one for himself and entrusted the other to his absent friend. And whenever either wished to write something rather secret to the other, he wrapped a white bird, that is, a sheet of papyrus, of small width but of the length of the doubled rod, around the wood, and tied it below and above with wax. Afterwards he wrote on the sheet, continuously from the sides joined artfully together into a mass, whatever he wished; then he loosened the sheet from the rod, and immediately there appeared such a distance between the letters that not even one word cohered with another. He turned the sheet, and when he wished he wrote to himself on the other side. Nor was there anyone ignorant of this device who could have investigated [unclear]. But the man who had the other rod, when he had received the sheet, fastened it on and recalled the letters into their former order.

Mystery. Marcus Tullius Cicero, eloquent orator of the Romans, using talent and art, changed the little elements of phrase into signs, and the rest.

Explanation. He wrote a book of signs for his son, which the blessed martyr Cyprian afterwards enlarged for the use of Christians, namely in the manner of a dictionary
